touches.text: A question is [Q#n: ...]. Its #n is its own and never changes; a new question takes the next unused number, which is 88. An answered question disappears: what stays is the answer and its why, written into the outline.

The ticket IS its own manager. It carries its workflow and status, and asks each gate whether it can transit. If refused, it gets itself back to design for fixing. If no handler is available to ask, it throws a trouble and waits until we decide. Design is CC and Akien. Akien, 2026-11-11, Q#85: "you and me. later there will be a specific agent for it, but that's so far off we're not even thinking about it now except 'after the outline is implemented'." So until then a refused ticket waits in the trouble lane, which both of us read when a session opens, and nothing posts to a design verb that no machine answers.

A ticket's code is a tool or machine; its life is data. All of its state is on disk, so anyone can instantiate it to talk to it, and any dialog is written to the relevant part of the ticket as it happens. To cross a gate the ticket asks that gate to queue it, sending only its fileref: devices/codemother/0/machines/<inspector>/queueme <fileref>. The gate instantiates the ticket from that fileref on its own side. A ticket instance then processes the pass or fail: on a pass it goes on to the next step, alerting the probes watching the gate (3.3.4.2); on a fail it asks design to queue it, the same way. Self-queuing is the abstract ticket's (3.3.2), so every kind inherits it and no caller queues a ticket on its behalf (Akien, same day: "that could be in the class, rather than the instance :) self queuing"). WHY: Akien, 2026-11-10: "now it has to send it's fileref over to the thing that will process it, and a new code instance created over there even tho it's the same thing... because that's good encapsulation. :)"

Ideas and questions are not tickets. An idea is a note that leads to an intention, and stops mattering once the intention is set down. A question exists only to deduce the why: once answered, what matters is the answer and the why, and nothing else.

Cross-domain questions (cognition questions): inherently cross domain, not domain specific. "How might that work?" is Akien's number one: "it's applicable in almost all domains, and captures the pattern, not the domain specific answer." They are not design questions: a design question is a spec choice waiting on Akien (cairn question, CairnCommons/questions/).

The corpus is a git JSON file beside the librarian's code (shareable spec, 4.3.4); the question trees are derived from it. Every entry carries its origin: verbatim (Akien's words, with date and source) or proposed (by CC, by Gemini, ...). All questions are included; the origin keeps his words apart. "i expect i have a couple of hundred in my own head."

Harvest: a deterministic pass over Akien's logs and notes proposes question-shaped lines in his words; he confirms each before it is marked verbatim. New ones are added through a librarian command as he says them.

Outline check: when a ticket is cast, the cheapest model reads it beside the outline sections it touches. A conflict, or an open question in those sections, becomes a question on the ticket, which holds its build until answered. It reads the outline as it stands each time, so editing the outline costs nothing.

artifact: the one door a record of truth changes through, and the journal of who came through it (hash-chained, caller read from the kernel). WHY: errors are permanent in records of truth (Law 7), and the journal is what shows a record moved by hand. USERS: everyone who writes a record.

question: the open-question door: a decision only the operator can make, bound to its ticket, answered in the operator's words. WHY: a spec choice is settled by Akien's head, recorded verbatim, never by a paragraph of CC's. USERS: tickets and CodeMother open them; the operator answers (7.4.2).
